newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada might phase in tobacco sponsorship rules.
newsitem.headline: Canada might phase in tobacco sponsorship rules.

text.p: Canadian Health Minister David Dingwall said on Wednesday he was willing to listen to requests to phase in controversial restrictions on tobacco sponsorship of sporting and arts events.

"I've heard representations and...I will look at it in the fullness of time. We have many weeks before we come back in February. I'll examine it as I'm going to examine a number of other things that have come to my attention," he said.
Speaking to reporters at Parliament, he was reacting to a request by Quebec officials to phase in or withdraw the restrictions on sponsorships.
But he did not voice much sympathy for the argument that it would hurt festivals, like motor racing in Montreal.

"There are 11,000 people in the province of Quebec each and every year from tobacco consumptions, 40,000 Canadians die each and every year, an unprecedented number of young people who are smoking in this country," he said. "That to me is of a paramount concern to the government of Canada and I believe to Canadians."
He added that smoking cost the government-funded health care system C$3.5 billion each year.

Dingwall had hoped to rush his anti-tobacco package, which restricts tobacco advertising and bans vending machine sales, through the House of Commons before it recesses for Christmas at the end of this week.
But Herb Gray, the minister who runs the government's legislative programme in the House, said it would not be further debated this week.
"I don't expect the tobacco bill to be before the House until we come back in February," he told reporters.
Once it passes the House -- as it is certain to do in some form, even if amended, given the Liberal government majority -- the bill will proceed to the unelected Senate, where it could face delays.
Dingwall said he was unable to predict whether the restrictions would be in place by the summer of 1997.
Canada's tobacco industry is about 65 percent-controlled by Imperial Tobacco Ltd, a unit of Imasco Ltd. Imasco is about 40 percent-owned by Britain's B.A.T. Industries Plc.
Another big Canadian cigarette company is Rothmans Inc -- a unit of Rothmans International Plc -- and 40 percent by Philip Morris and Cos Inc.
A third major player is RJR MacDonald, wholly-owned by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp unit R.J. Reynolds Tobacco International.
